passages.t: Locusts, fire and a plumb line
passages.happening:
The Lord GOD shows Amos swarms of locusts, made ready just after the king's harvest, as the late crop is coming up. When they have eaten every green thing, Amos prays, “Lord GOD, please forgive! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” (verse 2). ‘So the LORD relented from this plan’ (verse 3), and said it would not happen.

Then God shows him judgment by fire, consuming the great deep and devouring the land (verse 4). Amos prays again, “Lord GOD, please stop! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” (verse 5). Again the LORD relents (verse 6).

The third time, the Lord stands by a wall with a plumb line in his hand. He asks Amos what he sees, and Amos says, a plumb line. God says he is setting a plumb line among his people Israel and ‘I will no longer spare them’ (verse 8). The high places will be deserted, the sanctuaries laid waste, and God will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The king's harvest was probably the first cutting of hay or grain taken as tax for the royal stables. After it, the late spring crop was what the farmers had left to live on. Locusts at that moment would leave them with nothing. The fire that consumes the great deep pictures a heat so fierce that it seems to dry up the waters beneath the earth.

The first two visions follow one pattern: God shows, Amos pleads, God relents. Amos does not argue that Israel deserves mercy. He pleads its smallness. Then the third vision breaks the pattern. A plumb line is a weight on a cord used to check whether a wall stands straight, and a wall out of true must be pulled down. This time Amos does not pray, and God does not relent.

Verse 9 speaks against the house of Jeroboam, the dynasty. Jeroboam II died a natural death, but his son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was murdered, ending the dynasty by the sword as Amos had warned.
passages.later: Moses also pleaded for Israel, and ‘the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened’ (Exodus 32:14). Jeremiah heard the principle behind it: if a nation turns from its evil, God will relent of the disaster he planned (Jeremiah 18:7-8).
passages.hard:
If God relents in answer to prayer, does God change his mind?

The chapter says plainly that the LORD relented. Other passages say that God does not change his mind as people do (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Readers have held these together in several ways. Many classical theologians hold that God's purposes do not change and that texts like this describe God's action from the human side: God has determined to answer the prayers he himself prompts. Others, open theists among them, take the language more directly and argue that God truly responds to human action in time. A middle view stresses that God's warnings carry a condition within them, as Jeremiah 18 says, so relenting fits his unchanging character.

All agree that the text wants readers to believe that prayer matters to God.
passages.asks: Amos prayed for Israel because it was so small. Ask who you could plead for today, not because they deserve it, but because they cannot stand on their own. And ask where God's plumb line would find your life out of true.

passages.happening:
Amaziah the priest of Bethel sends word to King Jeroboam that Amos is plotting against him and that the land cannot bear his words (verse 10). He reports Amos as saying that Jeroboam will die by the sword and Israel will go into exile (verse 11). Then he tells Amos, “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there” (verse 12). Amos must never prophesy at Bethel again, ‘because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom’ (verse 13).

Amos answers that he was not a prophet or the son of a prophet, ‘rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees’ (verse 14). The LORD took him from following the flock and told him to go and prophesy to his people Israel (verse 15). Because Amaziah says not to prophesy against Israel, Amos gives him the LORD's word: disaster will fall on his own household and land, he will die in a foreign land, and Israel will go into exile (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
Bethel had been one of the two royal sanctuaries of the north since Jeroboam I set up a golden calf there, about 930 BC. Amaziah calls it the king's sanctuary and the temple of the kingdom: a state shrine, where the priest served at the king's pleasure. To him, a prophet who threatened the king's house was a political danger. His report even sharpens Amos's words. Amos had spoken against the house of Jeroboam; Amaziah reports that Jeroboam himself will die by the sword.

Earn your bread there suggests Amaziah thinks Amos is a professional prophet working for pay. Amos's answer is that he is not. Son of a prophet means a member of a guild of prophets, like the groups around Elijah and Elisha. Amos was a herdsman and a grower of sycamore figs, a cheap fruit eaten by the poor. Sycamore figs grow in warmer lowlands, not in the hills of Tekoa, so Amos may have owned or worked land elsewhere. He spoke because the LORD sent him.

The word against Amaziah in verse 17 describes what conquest would bring on a priest's household. These notes name it and do not dwell on it. It gives no one a warrant to wish harm on anyone's family. Its last line turns Amaziah's own report into Amos's verdict: Israel will go into exile.
passages.later: The sons of the prophets gathered around Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:3-5). Jeroboam II died and rested with his fathers (2 Kings 14:29), and his son Zechariah was murdered after six months (2 Kings 15:8-10).
passages.asks: Amaziah wanted religion that served the king. Ask whether you have ever wanted God's word to stay away from your own interests. And Amos spoke only because God sent him. Ask what it would cost you to say what you know God has said.
